𝜷=(−2,−2,0,2,2).{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(-2,-2,0,2,2)\;. (3.6)

3.1.2 The matter field sector

All of the models in the database have a massless spectrum which includes the gauge and matter spectrum of the MSSM. However, some models have additional massless fields at the Abelian locus, Sα=0S^{\alpha}=0, which can include additional vector-like pairs of Higgs doublets and one additional massless U⁡(1)U(1) gauge boson, related to the non-anomalous part of the 𝒥{\cal J} gauge symmetry. Masses for these fields may be generated by non-vanishing SαS^{\alpha} VEVs and for this reason such models have been included in the database.

Our example model has one additional massless U⁡(1)U(1) vector field as stated at the top of Fig. 2. Alternatively, this follows from the general result (2.31) and the fact that only three of the vectors 𝐤a{\bf k}_{a} in Eq. (3.4) are linearly independent. The matter field spectrum at the Abelian locus, Sα=0S^{\alpha}=0, can be read off from the database entry entitled “Downstairs spectrum” and, from Fig. 2, for our example model it is given by

𝟏𝟎3,𝟏𝟎4,𝟏𝟎5,𝟓¯1,2,2​𝟓¯4,5,H3,4,H¯3,4,H3,5,H¯3,5,S2,1,4​S4,2,4​S5,2,2​S4,3,2​S5,3,S4,5,S5,4.{\bf 10}_{3},{\bf 10}_{4},{\bf 10}_{5},\bar{\bf 5}_{1,2},2\bar{\bf 5}_{4,5},H_{3,4},\bar{H}_{3,4},H_{3,5},\bar{H}_{3,5},S_{2,1},4S_{4,2},4S_{5,2},2S_{4,3},2S_{5,3},S_{4,5},S_{5,4}\;. (3.7)

Here, we follow the notation introduced in the previous section. In particular, we have grouped the standard model particles into their standard S​U​(5)SU(5) representations for ease of notation. We recall that the subscripts indicate the 𝒥{\cal J} charge of a multiplet. For example, 𝟏𝟎3{\bf 10}_{3} denotes a 𝟏𝟎{\bf 10} multiplet of S​U​(5)SU(5) with 𝒥{\cal J} charge 𝐐⁡(𝟏𝟎3)=𝐞3{\bf Q}({\bf 10}_{3})={\bf e}_{3}, while 𝟓¯1,2\bar{\bf 5}_{1,2} denotes a 𝟓¯\bar{\bf 5} multiplet of S​U​(5)SU(5) with 𝒥{\cal J} charge 𝐐⁡(𝟓¯1,2)=𝐞1+𝐞2{\bf Q}(\bar{\bf 5}_{1,2})={\bf e}_{1}+{\bf e}_{2}. The 𝒥{\cal J} charge for a down Higgs is, for example, 𝐐⁡(H3,4)=𝐞3+𝐞4{\bf Q}(H_{3,4})={\bf e}_{3}+{\bf e}_{4} while we have 𝐐⁡(H¯3,4)=−𝐞3−𝐞4{\bf Q}(\bar{H}_{3,4})=-{\bf e}_{3}-{\bf e}_{4} for an up Higgs. The standard model singlet fields are denoted by SS and their 𝒥{\cal J} charge pattern is exemplified by 𝐐⁡(S2,1)=𝐞2−𝐞1{\bf Q}(S_{2,1})={\bf e}_{2}-{\bf e}_{1}.

The mixed 𝒥​GSM​GSM{\cal J}G_{\rm SM}G_{\rm SM} triangle anomaly can be computed from Eq. (2.28). For the above spectrum we easily find

𝐀=(1,1,3,5,5).{\bf A}=(1,1,3,5,5)\;. (3.8)

Further, using the values of the charge vectors (3.4) and of 𝜷{\boldsymbol{\beta}} in Eq. (3.6) it follows that

(kai​βi)a=(−2,−2,0,2,2).(k^{i}_{a}\beta_{i})_{a}=(-2,-2,0,2,2)\;. (3.9)

Therefore, the anomaly constraint (2.29) is indeed satisfied for our example model, as it must be due to the Green-Schwarz mechanism. This simple calculation provides a useful consistency check for our models.

The spectrum (3.7) shows that the example model contains two massless pairs of Higgs doublets at the locus Sα=0S^{\alpha}=0. In cases such as these a physical pair of Higgs doublets is chosen and separate models are generated for each possible choice. For the case at hand, the choice is H3,5H_{3,5}, H¯3,4\bar{H}_{3,4}, as the “Phys. Higgs” entry in Fig. 2 indicates. For consistency, the other Higgs doublet should then obtain a mass from non-zero singlet VEVs if we are to recover exactly the standard model charged spectrum with the chosen Higgs doublet. The relevant mass operators will be discussed in Section 3.1.5. Another possibility is, of course, to consider phenomenological models with two or three Higgs doublets.

In the following, we will discuss the various types of 𝒥{\cal J} invariant operators allowed in the effective action and their possible phenomenological relevance. For our example model, the relevant database entry listing these operators is shown in Fig. 3.

3.1.3 The D-terms

The general form of the D-term has been given in Eq. (2.24). The first term in this expression is the leading part of the FI term. Since we have already specified κ\kappa, for our example model given by Eq. (3.3), it suffices to provide the expressions kai​κik^{i}_{a}\kappa_{i} in order to fix this first term. In our database, these expressions are listed under the heading “FI-terms” and, from Fig. 3, for our example are given by

(kai​κi)=(−4​t1​t3−4​t2​t3+4​t1​t5+4​t2​t5+8​t4​t5+8​t52−4​t1​t2−8​t1​t4−8​t2​t4−4​t1​t5−4​t2​t5+8​t3​t5−8​t4​t5−4​t1​t2+4​t1​t3+4​t2​t3−8​t1​t4−8​t2​t4−8​t1​t5−8​t2​t5+8​t3​t5−16​t4​t5−8​t524​t1​t2−4​t1​t3+4​t2​t3+4​t1​t4+12​t2​t4+8​t2​t5−8​t3​t5+8​t4​t54​t1​t2+4​t1​t3−4​t2​t3+12​t1​t4+4​t2​t4+8​t1​t5−8​t3​t5+8​t4​t5).(k^{i}_{a}\kappa_{i})=\left(\begin{array}[]{l}-4t_{1}t_{3}-4t_{2}t_{3}+4t_{1}t_{5}+4t_{2}t_{5}+8t_{4}t_{5}+8t_{5}^{2}\\ -4t_{1}t_{2}-8t_{1}t_{4}-8t_{2}t_{4}-4t_{1}t_{5}-4t_{2}t_{5}+8t_{3}t_{5}-8t_{4}t_{5}\\ -4t_{1}t_{2}+4t_{1}t_{3}+4t_{2}t_{3}-8t_{1}t_{4}-8t_{2}t_{4}-8t_{1}t_{5}-8t_{2}t_{5}+8t_{3}t_{5}-16t_{4}t_{5}-8t_{5}^{2}\\ 4t_{1}t_{2}-4t_{1}t_{3}+4t_{2}t_{3}+4t_{1}t_{4}+12t_{2}t_{4}+8t_{2}t_{5}-8t_{3}t_{5}+8t_{4}t_{5}\\ 4t_{1}t_{2}+4t_{1}t_{3}-4t_{2}t_{3}+12t_{1}t_{4}+4t_{2}t_{4}+8t_{1}t_{5}-8t_{3}t_{5}+8t_{4}t_{5}\end{array}\right)\;. (3.10)

In order to specify the dilaton-dependent correction to the FI-term, which corresponds to the second term in Eq. (2.24), we need to provide the vector (kai​βi)a(k^{i}_{a}\beta_{i})_{a}. For the example model, this vector has already been determined from other database entries and is given in Eq. (3.9). Finally, we need the last term in Eq. (2.24) which represents the matter field contribution. Here, we write down the parts of these matter field D-terms which depend only on the singlet fields SαS^{\alpha}. In the database it is listed under the heading “singlet D-terms”. Fig. 3 shows that for our example model it is given by

(∑α,β¯qa​α​Sα​S¯β¯)=(−S2,1​S2,1†S2,1​S2,1†−S4,2​S4,2†−S5,2​S5,2†−S4,3​S4,3†−S5,3​S5,3†S4,2​S4,2†+S4,3​S4,3†+S4,5​S4,5†−S5,4​S5,4†−S4,5​S4,5†+S5,2​S5,2†+S5,3​S5,3†+S5,4​S5,4†).\left(\sum_{\alpha,\bar{\beta}}q_{a\alpha}S^{\alpha}\bar{S}^{\bar{\beta}}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}-S_{2,1}S^{\dagger}_{2,1}\\ S_{2,1}S^{\dagger}_{2,1}-S_{4,2}S^{\dagger}_{4,2}-S_{5,2}S^{\dagger}_{5,2}\\ -S_{4,3}S^{\dagger}_{4,3}-S_{5,3}S^{\dagger}_{5,3}\\ S_{4,2}S^{\dagger}_{4,2}+S_{4,3}S^{\dagger}_{4,3}+S_{4,5}S^{\dagger}_{4,5}-S_{5,4}S^{\dagger}_{5,4}\\ -S_{4,5}S^{\dagger}_{4,5}+S_{5,2}S^{\dagger}_{5,2}+S_{5,3}S^{\dagger}_{5,3}+S_{5,4}S^{\dagger}_{5,4}\end{array}\right)\;. (3.11)

In writing these expressions, we have omitted the Kahler moduli space metric of the singlet fields which should appear but is not explicitly known. However, for the analysis of D-flat directions with Sα≠0S^{\alpha}\neq 0 is it usually sufficient to know that this metric is positive definite.

At the locus Sα=0S^{\alpha}=0 where all singlet VEVs vanish, the systems we consider in this paper admit a solution to the D-term equations. A necessary condition for this to be possible is that the basic constraint (2.27) holds, that is, that we have more Kahler moduli than linearly independent charge vectors 𝐤a{\bf k}_{a}. For our example model, which has five Kahler moduli and three linearly independent charge vectors, this is certainly satisfied. Note also that, since the overall scaling of the Kähler moduli does not enter the D-term equations, such a solution can always be scaled to the large volume regime (that is, the regime where all values of the Kahler moduli tit^{i} are large).

For non-vanishing singlet VEVs, Sα≠0S^{\alpha}\neq 0, the existence of D-flat directions depends on the details of the above singlet matter field terms in the D-term and has to be analyzed case by case. Of course, for supersymmetric vacua with Sα≠0S^{\alpha}\neq 0 we also need to check the F-term equations which follow from the singlet superpotential WsingW_{\rm sing} in Eq. (2.9). We now turn to a discussion of this singlet superpotential.

3.1.4 The singlet superpotential: F-terms and Neutrino Majorana masses

In the database, the singlet superpotential is denoted by WsingW_{\rm sing}. A quick glance at Fig. 3 shows that for the example model it is given as

Wsing∼S4,52​S5,42,W_{\rm sing}\sim S_{4,5}^{2}S_{5,4}^{2}\;, (3.12)

with possible higher dimension operators omitted. It is important to note that the singlet fields with a given 𝒥{\cal J} charge can appear with multiplicity greater than one, as is evident from the spectrum (3.7). For simplicity, the sum over these multiplicities has been suppressed in the above expression. We also re-iterate from our general discussion in the previous section, that 𝒥{\cal J}-invariance of singlet operators does not necessarily imply their presence in WsingW_{\rm sing}, as they might be forbidden for other reasons. An example of this is provided by the gauge-invariant quadratic terms in the singlets, S4,5​S5,4S_{4,5}S_{5,4} for our example model. We know these terms must vanish since the underlying string construction shows that all of the singlets are indeed massless at the locus Sα=0S^{\alpha}=0. Given the uncertainty in the exact coefficients of the terms it is not possible to give an explicit solution to the F-terms where the contribution of one operator cancels against another. However, one can argue for the existence of such a solution assuming generic coefficients. It is also possible to show that, for a given combination of singlet VEVs, the contribution of each operator to the F-terms vanishes separately. For the above example (3.12) it is clear that the (global) singlet F-terms vanish as long as the VEVs of either S4,5S_{4,5} or S5,4S_{5,4} are zero.

The standard model singlet fields are also attractive candidates for right-handed neutrinos (RHNs). In this context, the role of the singlet superpotential is to generate Majorana masses for the RHNs due to non-vanishing singlet VEVs . For example, for the superpotential (3.12) a non-zero VEV for S5,4S_{5,4} (with the VEV of S4,5S_{4,5} still vanishing to satisfy the F-term equations) generates a Majorana mass term for S4,5S_{4,5} which might then play the role of a RHN. Of course a realisation of the see-saw mechanism also requires the presence of an associated Dirac mass. This will be discussed in Section 3.1.8.

3.1.5 The Higgs sector

The only part of the spectrum charged under the standard model that varies within the database is the Higgs sector - some examples contain more than one set of Higgs doublets. For such models we identify a particular pair of weak doublets to play the role of the Higgs fields. This pair will then be used to calculate all of the relevant phenomenological operators such as the Yukawa couplings. The remaining doublets will be considered as exotic fields which must obtain a large mass. Another option would be to consider theories with multiple light Higgs doublet pairs. To cover all possibilities, we have generated a separate database entry for each possible choice of a Higgs doublet pair among the available doublets. The most straightforward way for the additional doublets to obtain a mass is through couplings of the form μi​j​(S)​Hi​H¯j\mu_{ij}(S)H^{i}\bar{H}^{j}. To study these couplings, for models with multiple doublet pairs, the database contains the 3×33\times 3 mass matrix μi​j\mu_{ij} for up to 3 pairs of Higgs fields. For our example model in Fig. 3 this matrix is given by

μi​j=({1,S4,5​S5,4,S4,52​S5,42}{S4,5,S4,52​S5,4,S4,53​S5,42}{0}{S5,4,S4,5​S5,42,S4,52​S5,43}{1,S4,5​S5,4,S4,52​S5,42}{0}{0}{0}{0}).\mu_{ij}=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}\left\{1,S_{4,5}S_{5,4},S_{4,5}^{2}S_{5,4}^{2}\right\}&\left\{S_{4,5},S_{4,5}^{2}S_{5,4},S_{4,5}^{3}S_{5,4}^{2}\right\}&\{0\}\\ \left\{S_{5,4},S_{4,5}S_{5,4}^{2},S_{4,5}^{2}S_{5,4}^{3}\right\}&\left\{1,S_{4,5}S_{5,4},S_{4,5}^{2}S_{5,4}^{2}\right\}&\{0\}\\ \{0\}&\{0\}&\{0\}\end{array}\right)\;. (3.13)

For the case at hand one row and one column vanish because the model only contains two doublet pairs. Our notation is such that each matrix entry (i,j)(i,j) lists singlet operator which can couple to Hi​H¯jH^{i}\bar{H}^{j} in a 𝒥{\cal J}-invariant way. The indices i,ji,j run over the massless doublet pairs in the order in which they are given in the spectrum (3.7). For a given singlet VEVs it is possible to study if the additional doublets can indeed obtain a large mass while keeping the chosen Higgs pair light. The diagonal entries in the above matrix contain entries 11, consistent with the 𝒥{\cal J}-invariance of the operator Hi​H¯iH^{i}\bar{H}^{i}. However, these entries should be ignored since, by construction, all doublets are indeed exactly massless at the locus Sα=0S^{\alpha}=0. This is another example of a set of operators absent for reasons unrelated to 𝒥{\cal J}-invariance.

Keeping models with multiple Higgs pairs in the database (while we did not keep models with additional massless matter which could similarly be made massive by GUT singlets) is primarily motivated by the possibility of realising an approximate UPQ​(1)U_{\rm PQ}(1) symmetry. As will be discussed in detail in section 4.1, for the simplest cases which we have scanned over, a single Higgs pair is always vector-like under 𝒥{\cal J} so that the 𝒥{\cal J}-symmetry does not contain a U​(1)P​QU(1)_{PQ} symmetry. However, such a symmetry may may be useful for forbidding proton decay operators, for generating attractive flavour structures, and for additional control over the Higgs mass. Given two pairs of doublets, where each pair has different 𝒥{\cal J} charges, it is possible to identify an off-diagonal combination as the Higgs fields thereby inducing a U​(1)P​QU(1)_{PQ}. Indeed, this has been done for the example model in Fig. 2 where H3,5H_{3,5}, H¯3,4\bar{H}_{3,4} has been chosen as the physical Higgs pair. Of course the remaining doublets, H¯3,5\bar{H}_{3,5} and H3,4H_{3,4} in the example, must obtain a mass due which breaks the U​(1)P​QU(1)_{PQ} symmetry. If this breaking is sufficiently controlled, for example due to a breaking scale well below the string scale, the remaining approximate U​(1)P​QU(1)_{PQ} symmetry might still be useful.

For the example model, a VEV for S4,5S_{4,5} gives mass to the additional doublets while keeping the physical Higgs fields massless.

3.1.6 Yukawa Couplings

The database contains the Yukawa couplings under the headings Y(u)Y^{(u)} and Y(d)Y^{(d)}. For the example model in Fig. 3 they are given by

Y(u)\displaystyle Y^{(u)} =\displaystyle= ({S5,3,S4,3​S5,4,S4,5​S5,3​S5,4}{S5,4,S4,5​S5,42}{1,S4,5​S5,4}{S5,4,S4,5​S5,42}{0}{0}{1,S4,5​S5,4}{0}{0})\displaystyle\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}\left\{S_{5,3},S_{4,3}S_{5,4},S_{4,5}S_{5,3}S_{5,4}\right\}&\left\{S_{5,4},S_{4,5}S_{5,4}^{2}\right\}&\left\{1,S_{4,5}S_{5,4}\right\}\\ \left\{S_{5,4},S_{4,5}S_{5,4}^{2}\right\}&\{0\}&\{0\}\\ \left\{1,S_{4,5}S_{5,4}\right\}&\{0\}&\{0\}\end{array}\right)
Y(d)\displaystyle Y^{(d)} =\displaystyle= ({S5,3,S4,3​S5,4,S4,5​S5,3​S5,4}{0}{0}{S5,4,S4,5​S5,42}{0}{0}{1,S4,5​S5,4}{0}{0}),\displaystyle\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}\left\{S_{5,3},S_{4,3}S_{5,4},S_{4,5}S_{5,3}S_{5,4}\right\}&\{0\}&\{0\}\\ \left\{S_{5,4},S_{4,5}S_{5,4}^{2}\right\}&\{0\}&\{0\}\\ \left\{1,S_{4,5}S_{5,4}\right\}&\{0\}&\{0\}\end{array}\right)\;,

where we have dropped terms higher than cubic in SαS^{\alpha}. For each model we also list the generic rank of these Yukawa matrices as in Fig. 2. For the above matrices we have rk⁡(Y(u))={2,2}{\rm rk}\left(Y^{(u)}\right)=\left\{2,2\right\} and rk⁡(Y(d))={1,1}{\rm rk}\left(Y^{(d)}\right)=\left\{1,1\right\}. Here, the first (second) entry denotes the generic rank if all Sα=0S^{\alpha}=0 (if all SαS^{\alpha} are non-zero). We note that a non-vanishing top Yukawa coupling of order one is possible in these models, even at the Abelian locus Sα=0S^{\alpha}=0.

3.1.7 Proton decay

Proton decay forms one of the classic constraints on extensions of the standard model. Dimension four proton decay operators are tightly constrained by experiments to have coefficients less that 10−610^{-6} for any combination of generation indices [54]. Often these are forbidden by imposing the R-parity of the MSSM. However, within the context of top-down model building from string theory, such an R-parity does not necessarily have to be realized. It is, therefore, important to consider whether such operators can be forbidden using the U⁡(1)U(1) symmetries of our models. The dimension four and five proton decay operators in (2.11) and (2.12) are denoted by λp​q​r\lambda_{pqr} and λp​q​r​s′\lambda^{\prime}_{pqrs}, respectively, and are listed under those headings in the database. For our example model they can be found in Fig. 3.

3.1.8 Bilinear R-parity violating operators and superpotential Neutrino Dirac masses

An important set of operators which relates directly to neutrino physics are operators of the type ρp​H¯​Lp\rho_{p}\bar{H}L^{p} which appear in the superpotential (2.11). Such R-parity violating operators, among other things, lead directly to large neutrino masses through mixing with the Higgs fields and so are constrained to be very small (around 10−2210^{-22} in Planck units). For the example model in Fig. 3 these coefficients vanish

ρ=(000).\rho=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}0\\ 0\\ 0\end{array}\right)\;. (3.22)

Therefore, in this case non-vanishing singlet VEVs cannot generate any R-parity violating operators. As ever, a bare quadratic term in the superpotential is forbidden by construction in these models.

If we take some of the standard model singlets to be RHNs then these same terms also play the role of the superpotential neutrino Dirac masses. These may then be combined with the pure singlet terms discussed in section 3.1.4 to realize the see-saw mechanism. For the example model no such superpotential Dirac masses are allowed.

3.1.9 Neutrino Kähler potential Dirac masses

In the absence of superpotential Dirac or Majorana neutrino masses there is a natural way to induce neutrino masses of the correct magnitude through a Kähler potential operator [55]. The relevant operator in the matter Kahler potential (2.19) is

ρ^p​Lp​H†.\hat{\rho}_{p}L^{p}H^{\dagger}\;. (3.23)

When the up-type Higgs develops a VEV, vv, it induces an F-term for the down-type Higgs which, from the above operator, leads to Dirac neutrino masses. For our example model in Fig. 3 these couplings are given by

ρ^=({0}{S4,5​S4,3†,S4,2​S4,3†​S5,2†,S4,5​S5,4​S5,3†}{S4,5​S4,3†,S4,2​S4,3†​S5,2†,S4,5​S5,4​S5,3†}).\hat{\rho}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\{0\}\\ \left\{S_{4,5}S^{\dagger}_{4,3},S_{4,2}S^{\dagger}_{4,3}S^{\dagger}_{5,2},S_{4,5}S_{5,4}S^{\dagger}_{5,3}\right\}\\ \left\{S_{4,5}S^{\dagger}_{4,3},S_{4,2}S^{\dagger}_{4,3}S^{\dagger}_{5,2},S_{4,5}S_{5,4}S^{\dagger}_{5,3}\right\}\end{array}\right)\;. (3.24)

Following the discussion in Section 3.1.4 we may consider S4,5S_{4,5} as a RHN. Then giving a VEV to S4,3S_{4,3} induces Dirac neutrino mass. Note that we allow for conjugates of the singlets to appear since we are dealing with a Kähler potential operator.

3.1.10 The Giudice-Masiero term

A well-known way to induce a μ\mu-term within gravity mediated supersymmetry breaking is through the Giudice-Masiero mechanism [56]. The relevant operator in the matter field Kahler potential (2.19) is

μ~​H​H¯.\tilde{\mu}H\bar{H}\;. (3.25)

If μ~\tilde{\mu} depends on the conjugate, Sα†S^{\alpha\dagger}, of a singlet field which breaks supersymmetry, a μ\mu-term of the right order of magnitude is generated. Hence, we should list all gauge invariant operators of the above form which involve at least one singlet appearing as a conjugate. For the example model in Fig. 3 this leads to the operators

μ~⊃{S4,5†,S5,2​S4,2†,S5,3​S4,3†,(S4,5†)2​S5,4†}.\tilde{\mu}\supset\left\{S^{\dagger}_{4,5},S_{5,2}S^{\dagger}_{4,2},S_{5,3}S^{\dagger}_{4,3},\left(S^{\dagger}_{4,5}\right)^{2}S^{\dagger}_{5,4}\right\}\;. (3.26)

3.1.11 Kinetic terms and soft masses

One of the useful properties of the U⁡(1)U(1) symmetries is that they allow us to gain a handle on the form of the kinetic terms of the matter fields. The kinetic terms enter the determination of the physical Yukawa couplings from the Yukawa couplings in the superpotential and are therefore of great importance. However, due to their non-holomorphic nature, they are rather difficult to calculate from first principles. For our example model in Fig. 3 we have

K(𝟓¯)\displaystyle K^{(\bar{\bf 5})} =\displaystyle= (1S2,1†​S4,2†​S5,2†S2,1†​S4,2†​S5,2†S2,1​S4,2​S5,211S2,1​S4,2​S5,211),\displaystyle\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}1&S^{\dagger}_{2,1}S^{\dagger}_{4,2}S^{\dagger}_{5,2}&S^{\dagger}_{2,1}S^{\dagger}_{4,2}S^{\dagger}_{5,2}\\ S_{2,1}S_{4,2}S_{5,2}&1&1\\ S_{2,1}S_{4,2}S_{5,2}&1&1\end{array}\right)\;,
K(𝟏𝟎)\displaystyle K^{({\bf 10})} =\displaystyle= (1S4,2S5,3S4,3†1S4,5†S5,3†S4,51).\displaystyle\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}1&S_{4,2}&S_{5,3}\\ S_{4,3}^{\dagger}&1&S_{4,5}^{\dagger}\\ S_{5,3}^{\dagger}&S_{4,5}&1\end{array}\right)\;.

For simplicity we have only displayed the leading term for each operator while Fig. 3 shows the full list including terms involving up to 3 standard model singlets.

The same gauge invariant combinations are also relevant for constraining the possible soft supersymmetry breaking masses that can appear in the potential. Understanding their flavour structure is important, especially within gravity mediation, due to the possibility of inducing flavour changing neutral currents (FCNCs). It is well known that it is possible to use U⁡(1)U(1) global symmetries to constrain the flavour off-diagonal terms of such soft masses and the structure of the operators in Eq. (3.1.11) will be conductive to realizing such a scenario.

3.2 General phenomenology overview of database

Having described the output data for an individual model it is interesting to consider how various basic phenomenological properties are distributed within the database as a whole. To this end, we present some statistics of models in the database. The given numbers are not meant as a comprehensive statistical analysis of heterotic line bundle models but merely as a rough indication of how difficult it might be to achieve certain phenomenological properties within this class.

The models presented in the database [42] descend from the 202 S​U​(5)SU(5) GUT models constructed in Ref. [35] by quotienting the Calabi-Yau three-fold and Wilson line breaking. This process breaks the GUT group to the standard model group and projects out certain unwanted states, in particular the Higgs triplets still present in the GUT theory. Depending on the symmetry by which we divide (either ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} or ℤ2×ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2} in all cases) there are between order 100 and 1000 choices per GUT model on how to realize this breaking. Not all of these choices lead to a phenomenologically viable spectrum (for example, in some cases Higgs triplets are still present) and, for a given model, many choices result in the same spectrum. In our scan, we have only kept the cases which lead to an acceptable spectrum and we have chosen one representative model per spectrum generated. This leads to a total of 21222122 line bundle standard models which originate from the 202 GUT models. A list of these models is available as a data file at [42]. Upon inspection it turns out that many of these models are closely related in that they have the same spectrum and are based on the same (or equivalent) Calabi-Yau manifolds and the same bundle. Two models related in this way look identical for the purposes of this paper, although, since they are generally based on different symmetries of the Calabi-Yau manifold, they may differ at a more detailed level. We have eliminated these redundancies in the explicit printout of the models, in order to keep the size manageable. This results in 407 models available in the printed lists at [42]. The statistics of phenomenological properties below is based on these 407 models.

The results are summarized in Table 1 below.

A few comments on what precisely is being counted are in order. The number of massless U⁡(1)U(1) vector fields and the number of Higgs pairs is determined at the Abelian locus Sα=0S^{\alpha}=0 where all singlet VEVs vanish. As discussed earlier, massless U⁡(1)U(1) vector bosons can acquire a mass when singlet VEVs are switched on. This means that the 170 models with such a massless vector boson are not necessarily ruled out but have to be analyzed in more detail. A similar remark applies to models with more than one Higgs pair. The rank of the up Yukawa matrix Y(u)Y^{(u)} in column six of the table has also been determined for vanishing singlet VEVs. It can be shown that the U⁡(1)U(1) symmetries in 𝒥{\cal J} never allow an up Yukawa matrix with rank one and, it turns out there are no examples with rk⁡(Y(u))=3{\rm rk}(Y^{(u)})=3 in our list. This means all 4545 models mentioned in column six have Y(u)=2Y^{(u)}=2 while all remaining models have an entirely vanishing up Yukawa matrix for vanishing singlet VEVs. A positive rank for Y(u)Y^{(u)} is, of course, desirable since we would like a top Yukawa coupling of order one, however, it would be preferable to have rk⁡(Y(u))=1{\rm rk}(Y^{(u)})=1. This can, in fact, be achieved for related constructions, to be discussed in the second part of the paper, which lead to fewer U⁡(1)U(1) symmetries in the low-energy theory.

The second last column in the table gives the number of models for which all proton decay operators in (2.11) and (2.12) vanish, that is, λp​q​r=0\lambda_{pqr}=0 and λp​q​r​s′=0\lambda^{\prime}_{pqrs}=0 for all values of the family indices and in the presence of generic singlet VEVs. Evidently, this is a fairly strong condition which is sufficient but not necessary to guarantee that such operators do not destabilize the proton. For example, some terms for the second and third family might be allowed, particularly if they are suppressed by small singlet VEVs. This has to be studied in detail on a case-by-case basis. At any rate, it is encouraging that we remain with 1313 models even when all conditions are imposed simultaneously, as in the last column of Table 1.

4 The Geometry of Split Heterotic Models

In this section, we introduce the necessary formalism to study compactifications of the E8×E8E_{8}\times E_{8} heterotic theory on smooth Calabi-Yau manifolds [2] and the associated low-energy particle physics. In particular, we will discuss split bundles, that is, bundles with a direct product structure group. Bundles of this type, with the simplest splitting into a structure group S⁡(U​(1)5)S(U(1)^{5}), underly the standard models presented in the first part of this paper. For reason which will become clear we will keep our discussion more general to cover all splittings into unitary factors. The construction of specific models based on this formalism will be presented in the next section.

4.1 General Formalism

We begin by briefly reviewing the structure and constraints of generic heterotic Calabi-Yau compactifications. The geometric data required to specify a heterotic Calabi-Yau compactification which preserves four-dimensional N=1N=1 supersymmetry consist of a Calabi-Yau three-fold, XX, two holomorphic, poly-stable vector bundles, VV and V~\tilde{V}, with zero slope over XX and a holomorphic curve CC with second homology class [C][C]. The two vector bundles are associated to the observable and hidden E8E_{8} sectors of the theory and their structure groups, HH and H~\tilde{H}, must be sub-groups of E8E_{8}. In the present paper we will take these structure groups to be S​U​(n)SU(n) (hence c1​(V)=0c_{1}(V)=0), typically with n=5n=5 for the observable sector, or sub-groups thereof. The holomorphic curve CC is wrapped by five-branes (NS five-branes in the weakly coupled limit, M five-branes in the 11-dimensional strong-coupling picture) whose other directions stretch across the four-dimensional uncompactified space-time.

This data has to satisfy a series of consistency conditions in order to obtain a well-defined vacuum. We will outline the conditions briefly here and study them in more depth in the following subsections. The first condition on the geometry is the well-known heterotic anomaly cancellation condition [2],

c2​(T​X)−c2​(V)−c2​(V~)=[C].c_{2}(TX)-c_{2}(V)-c_{2}(\tilde{V})=[C]\;. (4.1)

In the subsequent discussion, we will focus on the observable bundle VV. The hidden bundle V~\tilde{V} and the five-brane curve CC will not be constructed explicitly but we will ensure, by an appropriate choice of VV, that a consistent completion of the model exists. Usually, we will do this by requiring c2​(T​X)−c2​(V)c_{2}(TX)-c_{2}(V) to be an effective class, [C]∈H2​(X)[C]\in H_{2}(X). Hence, in this case we can obtain a consistent completion of the model by adding an appropriate amount of five-branes while choosing the hidden bundle V~\tilde{V} to be trivial.

The presence of the vector bundle VV (that is, the presence of non-trivial gauge field VEVs over the Calabi-Yau three-fold, XX) breaks the visible sector E8E_{8} symmetry to a sub-group, G⊂E8G\subset E_{8}. The gauge group, GG, is given by the commutant of HH in E8E_{8}. For example, choosing the structure group to be H=S​U​(5)H=SU(5) produces the commutant of G=S​U​(5)G=SU(5) so that we obtain a minimal GUT theory in four dimensions. If HH is a proper rank four sub-group of S​U​(5)SU(5), as we will consider in this paper, the low-energy gauge group enhances to G=S​U​(5)×𝒥G=SU(5)\times{\cal J}, where 𝒥≅U​(1)f−1{\cal J}\cong U(1)^{f-1} consists of a product of U⁡(1)U(1) factors. As will be reviewed in the following sections, it is well-known, that some or all of these U⁡(1)U(1) factors are anomalous in the Green-Schwarz sense and are, consequently, spontaneously broken at a high scale with associated massive vector bosons. The various types of low-energy multiplets in the GUT theory are obtained by decomposing the 𝟐𝟒𝟖{\bf 248} adjoint representation of E8E_{8} into representations of H×GH\times G and the number of each multiplet can be computed from the bundle-valued cohomology of VV and its tensor powers.

In order to produce realistic four-dimensional models, it is necessary to further break the GUT group to the Standard Model. To this end, we will also introduce Wilson lines. However, Wilson lines can only be defined over a Calabi-Yau manifold, XX, which is not simply connected (i.e. π1​(X)≠0\pi_{1}(X)\neq 0). Since there are few known Calabi-Yau geometries which have a non-trivial fundamental group by construction, we shall explicitly construct such manifolds from simply connected ones, by forming quotient manifolds X/ΓX/\Gamma where Γ\Gamma is a discrete group. To this end, we require the existence of a symmetry Γ\Gamma acting freely on the Calabi-Yau three-fold XX, so that the quotient X^=X/Γ\hat{X}=X/\Gamma is smooth and has a non-trivial first fundamental group (for example, for X/ℤnX/\mathbb{Z}_{n}, π1​(X)=ℤn\pi_{1}(X)=\mathbb{Z}_{n}). In order for the bundle, VV, to descend to a bundle, V^\hat{V}, on the quotient Calabi-Yau X^\hat{X} the group Γ\Gamma must act consistently on the bundle. This means, there must be a group action of Γ\Gamma on VV which commutes with the projection π:V→X\pi:V\to X and satisfies a certain co-cycle condition. Such a group action is referred to as an “equivariant structure” and a bundle that admits such a structure is called “equivariant” with respect to Γ\Gamma. In summary, the “downstairs” Calabi-Yau manifold X^\hat{X} is defined by a multi-sheeted cover q:X→X/Γq:X\to X/\Gamma and all vector bundles on X^\hat{X} can be pulled back to equivariant bundles V=q∗​V^V=q^{*}{\hat{V}} on XX. That is, if VV is equivariant, V^{\hat{V}} is well-defined on X^{\hat{X}}.

With the addition of non-trivial Wilson lines, the full “downstairs” bundle on X^\hat{X} is V^⊕𝒲\hat{V}\oplus{\cal W}, where 𝒲{\cal W} is a flat rank one bundle representing an Abelian Wilson line. Its structure group can be embedded into hypercharge UY​(1)⊂S​U​(5)U_{Y}(1)\subset SU(5) in order to break S​U​(5)SU(5) into the standard model group. The downstairs zero-mode spectrum can be obtained from the bundle cohomology of V^⊕𝒲\hat{V}\oplus{\cal W} which, in practice, can be computed from the cohomology of the upstairs bundle VV and its equivariant structure.

With this framework in hand, we turn now to the central point of this paper. We will consider vector bundles VV with a split structure group of the form

H=S⁡(U⁡(n1)×⋯×U⁡(nf)),H=S(U(n_{1})\times\dots\times U(n_{f}))\;, (4.2)

where na≥1n_{a}\geq 1 are integers. In order to ensure that the non-Abelian part of the low-energy gauge group is given by the GUT group S​U​(5)SU(5) we will demand that ∑a=1fna=5\sum_{a=1}^{f}n_{a}=5. We will be especially interested in the case of “maximal splitting” when na=1n_{a}=1 for all aa. In this case, VV is simply a direct sum of five line bundles, and S​U​(5)SU(5) splits as H=S⁡(U​(1)5)H=S(U(1)^{5}). However, other patterns will be of interest as well so that we keep the formalism general for now and characterize a particular pattern by the integer vector 𝐧=(n1,…,nf){\bf n}=(n_{1},\ldots,n_{f}). We will now explain in detail how the general formalism for heterotic Calabi-Yau compactifications outlined above applies to such split bundles. We begin with some simple group theoretical considerations.

4.2 Group theory

In this section we lay down the necessary notation to discuss both the gauge symmetries of the four-dimensional theory, as well as the structure group of the visible sector bundle, VV. We will find it convenient to introduce two sub-groups of the bundle structure group HH, namely the maximal semi-simple subgroup HsH_{s} and the maximal Abelian sub-group 𝒥{\cal J}. Explicitly, they are given by

Hs=S​U​(n1)×⋯×S​U​(nf),𝒥≅{(ei​η1,…,ei​ηf)|∑ana​ηa=0}≅U​(1)f−1,H_{s}=SU(n_{1})\times\dots\times SU(n_{f})\;,\quad{\cal J}\cong\{(e^{i\eta^{1}},\ldots,e^{i\eta^{f}})|\sum_{a}n_{a}\eta^{a}=0\}\cong U(1)^{f-1}\;, (4.3)

where ηa\eta^{a} are the U⁡(1)U(1) group parameters and the sum condition in the definition of 𝒥{\cal J} accounts for the fact that HH consists of special unitary matrices. The different possible splittings of S​U​(5)SU(5), together with the sub-groups HsH_{s} and 𝒥{\cal J} are listed in Table 2.

For the subsequent discussion it will be useful to label representations of the group HH by the HsH_{s} and 𝒥{\cal J} representations they induce. We denote by ℱa{\cal F}_{a} (Adja{\rm Adj}_{a}) the representation of HsH_{s} which transforms as a fundamental (adjoint) of the S​U​(na)SU(n_{a}) factor in HsH_{s} and as a singlet under all other factors. Representations of 𝒥{\cal J} are specified by a charge vector 𝐪=(q1,…,qf){\bf q}=(q_{1},\ldots,q_{f}). As a consequence of the constraint in the definition (4.3) of 𝒥{\cal J}, in order to get a one-to-one correspondence between charge vectors and 𝒥{\cal J} representations, we have to identify two such vectors 𝐪{\bf q} and 𝐪~\tilde{\bf q} if

𝐪−𝐪~∈ℤ​𝐧.{\bf q}-\tilde{\bf q}\in\mathbb{Z}{\bf n}\;. (4.4)

Finally, an HH representation which transforms under the representation RR of HsH_{s} and carries 𝒥{\cal J} charge 𝐪{\bf q} is denoted by R𝐪R_{\bf q}. Using this notation we can write down rules for the branching of S​U​(5)SU(5) representations into HH representations. For the S​U​(5)SU(5) representations relevant to our discussion these branching rules read explicitly

𝟏𝟎→(⨁a=1f(∧2ℱa)2​𝐞a)⊕(⨁a<b(ℱa⊗ℱb)𝐞a+𝐞b)𝟓¯→⨁a=1f(ℱ¯a)−𝐞a𝟏𝟎¯→(⨁a=1f(∧2ℱ¯a)−2​𝐞a)⊕(⨁a<b(ℱ¯a⊗ℱ¯b)−𝐞a−𝐞b)𝟓→⨁a=1f(ℱa)𝐞a𝟐𝟒→⨁a(Adja)𝟎⊕⨁a≠b(ℱa⊗ℱ¯b)𝐞a−𝐞b\begin{array}[]{lllllll}{\bf 10}&\rightarrow&(\bigoplus_{a=1}^{f}(\wedge^{2}{\cal F}_{a})_{2{\bf e}_{a}})\oplus(\bigoplus_{a<b}({\cal F}_{a}\otimes{\cal F}_{b})_{{\bf e}_{a}+{\bf e}_{b}})&&\bar{\bf 5}&\rightarrow&\bigoplus_{a=1}^{f}(\bar{{\cal F}}_{a})_{-{\bf e}_{a}}\\ \bar{\bf 10}&\rightarrow&(\bigoplus_{a=1}^{f}(\wedge^{2}\bar{{\cal F}}_{a})_{-2{\bf e}_{a}})\oplus(\bigoplus_{a<b}(\bar{{\cal F}}_{a}\otimes\bar{{\cal F}}_{b})_{-{\bf e}_{a}-{\bf e}_{b}})&&{\bf 5}&\rightarrow&\bigoplus_{a=1}^{f}({\cal F}_{a})_{{\bf e}_{a}}\\ {\bf 24}&\rightarrow&\bigoplus_{a}({\rm Adj}_{a})_{{\bf 0}}\oplus\bigoplus_{a\neq b}({\cal F}_{a}\otimes\bar{{\cal F}}_{b})_{{\bf e}_{a}-{\bf e}_{b}}&&&&\end{array} (4.5)

where 𝐞a{\bf e}_{a} denotes the atha^{\rm th} standard unit vector.

Let us now embed HH into E8E_{8} via the embedding chain H⊂S​U​(5)⊂E8H\subset SU(5)\subset E_{8}. The commutant of the so-embedded HH within E8E_{8}, that is the low-energy gauge group, is given by G=S​U​(5)×𝒥G=SU(5)\times{\cal J}. As discussed before, the U⁡(1)U(1) factors in 𝒥{\cal J} may be Green-Schwarz anomalous in which case their associated gauge bosons are massive. In order to find the multiplet types in the resulting S​U​(5)SU(5) GUT theory we need to decompose the 𝟐𝟒𝟖{\bf 248} adjoint representation of E8E_{8}. We begin with its well-known branching under S​U​(5)×S​U​(5)SU(5)\times SU(5) given by

𝟐𝟒𝟖→(𝟏,𝟐𝟒)⊕(𝟐𝟒,𝟏)⊕(𝟏𝟎,𝟓¯)⊕(𝟓,𝟏𝟎)⊕(𝟏𝟎¯,𝟓)⊕(𝟏𝟎¯,𝟓¯).{\bf 248}\rightarrow({\bf 1},{\bf 24})\oplus({\bf 24},{\bf 1})\oplus({\bf 10},\bar{\bf 5})\oplus({\bf 5},{\bf 10})\oplus(\bar{\bf 10},{\bf 5})\oplus(\bar{\bf 10},\bar{\bf 5})\;. (4.6)

Here, we think of the first S​U​(5)SU(5) as the internal and the second S​U​(5)SU(5) as the external gauge group. If we replace the internal S​U​(5)SU(5) representations with the branching rules in (4.5) we immediately obtain the desired branching of 𝟐𝟒𝟖{\bf 248} into representations of H×S​U​(5)H\times SU(5). The resulting multiplets together with other relevant information are listed in Table 3.

4.3 Split bundles and stability

We would like to construct vector bundles VV with the required structure group H=S⁡(U⁡(n1)×⋯×U⁡(nf))H=S(U(n_{1})\times\dots\times U(n_{f})). Starting with vector bundles UaU_{a} on the Calabi-Yau three-fold XX, each with structure group U⁡(na)U(n_{a}), we set

V=⨁a=1fUa.V=\bigoplus_{a=1}^{f}U_{a}\;. (4.7)

In order to ensure that the structure group is special unitary we also impose the vanishing of the first Chern class 33 3 If there are additional conditions between the first Chern classes of the UaU_{a} the structure group might reduce further and become a proper sub-group of one of the structure groups given in Table 2. In this case, the non-Abelian part of the low-energy gauge group might be larger than S​U​(5)SU(5). We will not consider this case explicitly in our general set-up and avoid models of this type in our discussion of examples later on.

c1​(V)=∑a=1fc1​(Ua)=!0.c_{1}(V)=\sum_{a=1}^{f}c_{1}(U_{a})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle!}}{{=}}0\;. (4.8)

Relative to a basis {ωi}\{\omega_{i}\} of harmonic two-forms on XX, where i=1,…,h1,1​(X)i=1,\ldots,h^{1,1}(X), we expand the first Chern classes as c1​(Ua)=c1i​(Ua)​ωic_{1}(U_{a})=c_{1}^{i}(U_{a})\omega_{i} and, in order to make contact with the four-dimensional discussion in the previous section, introduce the vectors 𝐤a{\bf k}_{a} by setting

kai=c1i​(Ua).k_{a}^{i}=c_{1}^{i}(U_{a})\;. (4.9)

Now we need to discuss the conditions on such bundles VV which follow from the requirement of preserving four-dimensional N=1N=1 supersymmetry. As discussed above, in order for this bundle to be supersymmetric, it needs to be poly-stable with zero slope.

To understand these conditions, we must define the notions of slope, stability and poly-stability which we introduce in turn. The slope μ⁡(𝒢)\mu({\cal G}) of a coherent sheaf, 𝒢{\cal G}, on the Calabi-Yau three-fold XX is defined by

μ⁡(𝒢)=1rk⁡(𝒢)​∫Xc1​(𝒢)∧J∧J=1rk⁡(𝒢)​di​j​k​c1i​(𝒢)​tj​tk,\mu({\cal G})=\frac{1}{{\rm rk}({\cal G})}\int_{X}c_{1}({\cal G})\wedge J\wedge J=\frac{1}{{\rm rk}({\cal G})}d_{ijk}c_{1}^{i}({\cal G})t^{j}t^{k}\;, (4.10)

where JJ is the Kahler form of XX. For the second equality we have expanded J=ti​ωiJ=t^{i}\omega_{i} and c1​(𝒢)=c1i​(𝒢)​ωic_{1}({\cal G})=c_{1}^{i}({\cal G})\omega_{i} and introduced the triple intersection numbers di​j​k=∫Xωi∧ωj∧ωkd_{ijk}=\int_{X}\omega_{i}\wedge\omega_{j}\wedge\omega_{k} of XX. A holomorphic vector bundle VV is now called (slope-) stable if

μ⁡(𝒢)<μ⁡(V)​for all coherent sub-sheaves​𝒢⊂V​with​0<rk⁡(𝒢)<rk⁡(V).\mu({\cal G})<\mu(V)~~\text{for all coherent sub-sheaves}~{\cal G}\subset V~~\text{with}~0<{\rm rk}({\cal G})<{\rm rk}(V)\;. (4.11)

Note that due to the restriction on the rank in this definition line bundles are always stable. Further, VV is called poly-stable if

V=⨁aVa​such that​Va​stable and​μ​(Va)=μ⁡(V)​∀aV=\bigoplus_{a}V_{a}~~\text{such that}~V_{a}~\text{stable and}~~\mu(V_{a})=\mu(V)~\forall a (4.12)

Hence, a poly-stable bundle consists of a direct sum of stable bundles, each with the same slope. Since supersymmetry also requires that μ⁡(V)=0\mu(V)=0 (which is automatic in our case since we consider bundles VV with c1​(V)=0c_{1}(V)=0) this means that the slope of all constituent bundles VaV_{a} must vanish. A poly-stable bundle VV with zero slope has no global sections since the trivial line bundle 𝒪X{\cal O}_{X} has slope zero and is, hence, a potentially de-stabilising sub-bundle. Therefore, 𝒪X{\cal O}_{X} cannot inject into VV and we must have H0​(X,V)≅Hom⁡(𝒪X,V)=0H^{0}(X,V)\cong{\rm Hom}({\cal O}_{X},V)=0. If VV is poly-stable, its dual V∗V^{*}, is also poly-stable with zero slope, so that on a Calabi-Yau manifold H3​(X,V)≅H0​(X,V∗)=0H^{3}(X,V)\cong H^{0}(X,V^{*})=0. In conclusion, poly-stable bundles with slope zero on a Calabi-Yau manifold have vanishing zeroth and third cohomology44 4 If a line bundle appears in the sum (4.12) the above argument breaks down. However, in this case, one can still conclude that a poly-stable, zero slope bundle VV satisfies H0​(X,V)=H3​(X,V)=0H^{0}(X,V)=H^{3}(X,V)=0 by invoking the vanishing Theorem (1.24) in Ref. [57]. It states that a line bundle LL has no global sections if μ⁡(L)<0\mu(L)<0 (and, on a Calabi-Yau manifold, it has vanishing third cohomology if μ⁡(L)>0\mu(L)>0) somewhere in the Kahler cone of XX. Since we require that μ⁡(L)=0\mu(L)=0, all line bundles except the trivial one have points in the Kahler cone where μ⁡(L)>0\mu(L)>0 and μ⁡(L)<0\mu(L)<0, so that the theorem applies and H0​(X,L)=H3​(X,L)=0H^{0}(X,L)=H^{3}(X,L)=0. The one exception is the trivial bundle 𝒪X{\cal O}_{X} which has vanishing slope everywhere in the Kahler cone and satisfied H0​(X,𝒪X)=H3​(X,𝒪X)=1H^{0}(X,{\cal O}_{X})=H^{3}(X,{\cal O}_{X})=1. However, we are not interested in cases for which 𝒪X{\cal O}_{X} appears in the direct sum in (4.7) since this leads to the case of enhanced symmetry described in footnote 3. Hence, for our considerations, all line bundles LL will indeed have vanishing zeroth and third cohomology..

Let us now apply these general statements to the bundle VV in (4.7). For VV to be supersymmetric it needs to be poly-stable with zero slope which is equivalent to saying that all UaU_{a} must be stable with zero slope, μ⁡(Ua)=0\mu(U_{a})=0. Stability is automatic if UaU_{a} is a line bundle but has to be checked explicitly for higher-rank bundles (this can be carried out explicitly following the procedure outlined in Ref. [69, 46]). For the full bundle VV to be poly-stable, the stable loci for the various UaU_{a} must have a non-trivial intersection in the Kahler cone. On this intersection VV is poly-stable. The second condition for supersymmetry, the vanishing of the slope for each UaU_{a}, can from Eq. (4.10) be expressed as

μ⁡(Ua)∼kai​κi=0​∀a,\mu(U_{a})\sim k^{i}_{a}\kappa_{i}=0~~\forall a\;, (4.13)

where κi=di​j​k​tj​tk\kappa_{i}=d_{ijk}t^{j}t^{k} are “dual” Kahler moduli space coordinates. Hence, the vanishing slope conditions lead to additional constraints on the Kahler moduli space of XX which have to be combined with the ones following from stability. As can be seen from Eq. (2.24), in the four-dimensional effective theory all these constraints are enforced via D-terms associated to the anomalous U⁡(1)U(1) symmetries in 𝒥{\cal J} and additional anomalous U⁡(1)U(1) symmetries which may appear at particular loci in Kahler moduli space when one or more of the bundles UaU_{a} split up further [59]. The bundle is supersymmetric only in the part of the Kahler moduli space where all of these conditions are satisfied simultaneously. As is clear from Eq. (4.13), in order for a common solution to the zero slope conditions to exist it is necessary that

(number of lin. independent ​𝐤a)<h1,1​(X).(\mbox{number of lin.~independent }{\bf k}_{a})<h^{1,1}(X)\;. (4.14)

In the context of the four-dimensional discussion we have seen the same condition (2.27), for the case of purely Abelian splittings, appear from the D-term equations.

For Calabi-Yau three-folds with a small Hodge number h1,1​(X)h^{1,1}(X), the slope zero conditions (4.13) are an important model building constraint on the bundle, VV. For example, for h1,1​(X)=1h^{1,1}(X)=1 there are no solutions at all, while for h1,1​(X)=2h^{1,1}(X)=2 all first Chern classes 𝐤a{\bf k}_{a} must be multiples of each other.

As we have seen, stability and vanishing slope of each UaU_{a} implies that H0​(X,Ua)=H3​(X,Ua)=0H^{0}(X,U_{a})=H^{3}(X,U_{a})=0. This means the chiral asymmetries associated to the bundles UaU_{a} (that is the chiral asymmetry of the 𝟏𝟎{\bf 10} and 𝟏𝟎¯\bar{\bf 10} multiplets with charges ±𝐞a\pm{\bf e}_{a}) can be computed from the index, so that ind⁡(Ua)=−h1​(X,Ua)+h2​(X,Ua){\rm ind}(U_{a})=-h^{1}(X,U_{a})+h^{2}(X,U_{a}).

An analogous argument holds for ∧2V\wedge^{2}V and its index. To see this, note that if VV is a poly-stable bundle with slope zero then it follows that ∧2V\wedge^{2}V (and V⊗V∗V\otimes V^{*}) are also poly-stable with slope zero [70]. As a result, each indecomposable term, ∧2Ua,Ua⊗Ub\wedge^{2}U_{a},U_{a}\otimes U_{b} in ∧2V\wedge^{2}V is a properly stable bundle with slope zero. Following the same line of argument once again, such a term either has vanishing zeroth and third cohomology, or consists of a trivial bundle in which case its zeroth and third cohomologies are equal. Either way we have that ind(∧2Ua)=−h1(X,∧2Ua)+h2(X,∧2Ua){\rm ind}(\wedge^{2}U_{a})=-h^{1}(X,\wedge^{2}U_{a})+h^{2}(X,\wedge^{2}U_{a}) (and similarly for Ua⊗UbU_{a}\otimes U_{b}), so that the index counts the chiral asymmetry of 𝟓¯\bar{\bf 5} and 𝟓{\bf 5} multiplets with charges ±(𝐞a+𝐞b)\pm({\bf e}_{a}+{\bf e}_{b}).

4.4 Spectrum of GUT theory

As discussed above, the four-dimensional gauge group is S​U​(5)×𝒥SU(5)\times{\cal J}, where 𝒥≃U​(1)f−1{\cal J}\simeq U(1)^{f-1} consists of U⁡(1)U(1) factors which are normally Green-Schwarz anomalous. From Table 3, the multiplets r𝐪r_{\bf q} under this gauge group are given by

𝟏𝐞a−𝐞b,𝟓¯𝐞a+𝐞b,𝟏𝟎𝐞a,𝟓−𝐞a−𝐞b,𝟏𝟎¯−𝐞𝐚{\bf 1}_{{\bf e}_{a}-{\bf e}_{b}},\bar{\bf 5}_{{\bf e}_{a}+{\bf e}_{b}},{\bf 10}_{{\bf e}_{a}},{\bf 5}_{-{\bf e}_{a}-{\bf e}_{b}},\overline{\bf 10}_{-{\bf e}_{a}} (4.15)

where we recall that the sub-script indicates the 𝒥{\cal J} charge, an integer vector subject to the identification (4.4). The corresponding internal HH representation, R𝐪R_{\bf q}, for each of these multiplets is listed in the first column of Table 3. Given that the bundles UaU_{a} are associated to the HH-representations (ℱa)𝐞a({\cal F}_{a})_{{\bf e}_{a}}, the associated bundles for each of the multiplets r𝐪r_{\bf q} in (4.15) are easily worked out by first identifying the corresponding HH representation R𝐪R_{\bf q} and then taking appropriate tensor products of (ℱa)𝐞a({\cal F}_{a})_{{\bf e}_{a}}. The result for the associated bundles UR𝐪U_{R_{\bf q}} is listed in the third column of Table 3. The number, n⁡(r𝐪)n(r_{\bf q}) of multiplets with S​U​(5)×𝒥SU(5)\times{\cal J} representation r𝐪r_{\bf q} is then given by the first cohomology, H1​(X,UR𝐪)H^{1}(X,U_{R_{\bf q}}), of these associated bundle. Serre duality on a Calabi-Yau manifold implies that H1​(X,U)≅H2​(X,U∗)H^{1}(X,U)\cong H^{2}(X,U^{*}) for any bundle UU. Hence, the chiral asymmetries N⁡(r𝐪)=n⁡(r𝐪)−n⁡(r¯−𝐪)N(r_{\bf q})=n(r_{\bf q})-n(\bar{r}_{-{\bf q}}) can be expressed in terms in terms of the topological index of each respective bundle as
